problems.form_value: JoyCaption image captioning turns each exemplar into a structured text description; a FLUX.1-dev text-to-image model fine-tuned with LoRA in two stages (...) generates the variations
problems.source_says: Minor wording error. No coded value changes, and FLUX.1-dev as the image generator is right. Each prompt has two parts: a brief summary in trigger words (brand name, industry, styles, colors) drawn from the creative brief, and an open-form caption that JoyCaption writes from the exemplar image. JoyCaption writes only the caption. Suggested wording: 'Each exemplar's prompt joins a trigger-word brief summary from the creative brief with an open-form JoyCaption caption of the exemplar; FLUX.1-dev, fine-tuned with LoRA in two stages (...), generates the variations from that prompt.'
problems.quote: We construct structured logo descriptions using two complementary pieces: a brief summary that summarizes information from the creative brief and an open-form description of the original exemplar generated by image captioning models.
problems.locator: PDF p. 10 (printed p. 9), Section 3.1; PDF p. 11 (printed p. 10), Section 3.1 ('we employ an off-the-shelf image captioning model, JoyCaption'; 'We combine the brief summary and the description into a standardized textual prompt')

problems.where: S1 Variation(1) and Variation(4); S2 Variation
problems.form_value: S1 how_used: 'The researchers generated the variations in advance and showed them in a gallery (5 pages of 12, ranked by the original exemplars' ratings) that only assigned designers could open during the two-week contest.' Open question 1 asks whether a gallery that designers 'view but never operate' counts under criterion 1.
problems.source_says: Omission, not an error. No coded value is wrong. The paper never says whether Variation designers were told that the gallery images were AI-generated. Section 4.1 says Open and Variation designers were told that the ratings of the exemplars shown reflected their click-attractiveness, although the Variation galleries carried the originals' ratings. The Appendix A example brief (its condition is not stated) calls the gallery logos 'we previously collected'. Criterion 1 still holds, because the codebook's ideas_supplied role does not require that participants know the material is AI-made. Suggested addition to open question 1: 'The paper does not say whether designers knew the variations were AI-generated.'
problems.quote: To inspire you and help guide your designs, we provide ratings on logos that we previously collected in the gallery below. These ratings show how well logos attract clicks.
problems.locator: PDF p. 36 (printed p. 35), Appendix A brief; PDF p. 18 (printed p. 17), Section 4.1 ('for the Open and Variation conditions, that the ratings of exemplars shown in the galleries reflected their click-attractiveness'); full text searched for told, informed, disclos, aware, unfamiliar

confirmed.statement: The document states random assignment for S1 three times. Introduction: 'We randomize designers’ access to logo exemplars in a creative brief across four treatment arms'. Section 4.1: 'participants were randomly assigned to receive access to a gallery, with each gallery corresponding to one experimental condition'. Figure 4 notes: 'Upon registration, designers were randomized into one of four conditions'. The form's S1 quote is the Figure 4 note, verbatim, and both locators are right (printed p. n = PDF p. n+1).
confirmed.locator: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 4); PDF p. 17 (printed p. 16), Section 4.1; PDF p. 19 (printed p. 18), Figure 4 notes

confirmed.statement: S1 assigns AI-generated material for the designer's own work. Every designer creates a new logo for the same brand, and the arms differ only in the gallery shown with the brief. Variation(1) shows 'one AI variation (created by our model) for each of the 60 pre-seeded exemplars, alongside the original exemplars’ ratings'. Variation(4) shows 'three additional variations per exemplar beyond the Variation(1) stimuli'. No arm differs only in whose output gets evaluated.
confirmed.locator: PDF p. 17 (printed p. 16), Section 4.1; PDF p. 19 (printed p. 18), Figure 4 notes

confirmed.statement: The tool is a generative image model. Section 3.2: 'we fine-tune a pre-trained T2I model, FLUX.1-dev, using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA)'. The introduction calls the stimuli 'AI-generated variations of original exemplars'. The gallery was a fixed set provided 'from the outset', and no designer ran the model, so role ideas_supplied fits the codebook. The Logo LoRA data (about 25,000 logo images from past restaurant contests on a crowdsourcing platform) and the 50 survey-rated pairs with a contrastive loss for the Optimization LoRA match the form.
confirmed.locator: PDF p. 11 (printed p. 10), Section 3.2; PDF p. 5 (printed p. 4); PDF p. 18 (printed p. 17); PDF pp. 12-16 (printed pp. 11-15), Sections 3.2.1 and 3.2.2

confirmed.statement: The S1 comparison arms match the form. Blind 'received only the contest brief, with no access to pre-seeded exemplars or their variations' (none). Open saw 'the 60 pre-seeded exemplars and their quality rating', logos the brand obtained 'in a private crowdsourcing design contest in 2019' (other_aid, which the form spec defines to include human-written examples). Variation(4) is included 'to test whether including more variations per exemplar can further improve contest outcomes compared to Variation(1)' (ai_design, with Variation(1) as the default).
confirmed.locator: PDF p. 17 (printed p. 16), Section 4.1 and footnote 1; PDF p. 18 (printed p. 17); form-spec.md, note on arms[].ai

confirmed.statement: S1 assigns individual designers between subjects. Each designer is counted in one condition, and 'Access to the galleries is restricted to assigned designers based on their designer IDs.' No designer works under two conditions, so check (e) on condition order does not apply.
confirmed.locator: PDF p. 18 (printed p. 17), Section 4.1; PDF p. 20 (printed p. 19), Table 1

confirmed.statement: The S1 counts match Table 1: registered 105, 105, 120, and 110 (Open, Variation(1), Variation(4), Blind; 440 in total) and participating 70, 71, 76, and 75 (292). The Table 1 notes define registered designers as those who viewed the contest information and creative brief, and the Figure 4 notes place randomization at registration, so 440 is the randomized count.
confirmed.locator: PDF p. 20 (printed p. 19), text and Table 1; PDF p. 19 (printed p. 18), Figure 4 notes

confirmed.statement: S2 states randomization by reference and through its balance tests. Section 5: 'We closely followed the experimental design from Section 4' and 'Randomization checks, presented in Web Appendix D, confirm there are no significant differences in demographics or participation across conditions'. D.1: 'We conduct a randomization check by doing t-tests for each variable separately'. Section 5 does not restate the unit or timing of randomization, and D.1 tests only the attributes of participating designers, with no printed test of participation. The form records the timing gap.
confirmed.locator: PDF p. 29 (printed p. 28), Section 5; PDF p. 65 (WA-21), D.1; PDF p. 66 (WA-22), Table WA-D.1

confirmed.statement: The S2 arms match the form: Open ('full exposure to 60 rated exemplars of varying quality'), Blind ('no exemplar exposure'), and Variation ('exposure to four variations per exemplar', the Variation(4) condition kept from Section 4, whose variations are 'created by our model'). Table 2 counts: registered 155, 161, and 169 (485); participating 65, 64, and 79 (208). Section 5 does not say where the S2 exemplars came from, so 'original' and other_aid for Open rest on the paper's general use of exemplars as the source designs that the AI varies.
confirmed.locator: PDF p. 29 (printed p. 28), Section 5 and Table 2; PDF p. 17 (printed p. 16), Section 4.1

confirmed.statement: No preregistration, trial registry, ethics review, or consent statement appears anywhere in the 69 pages, so preregistered = not_stated is right for both studies.
confirmed.locator: Main text, Appendix A-E, and Web Appendix A-D (PDF pp. 1-69), read and searched

summary: The PDF supports the assignment coding: Study 1 says three times that individual designers were randomized (PDF pp. 5, 17, 19) to no gallery, a gallery of the brand's human-made exemplars, or a gallery of one or four FLUX.1-dev variations per exemplar while they designed their own logo, and Study 2 follows that design with stated randomization checks (PDF pp. 29, 65), so criterion 1 holds. The refutation rests on detail only: ai_tool.name_model credits JoyCaption with the whole structured prompt, which the paper builds from a brief summary plus a JoyCaption caption, and the form does not record that the paper never says designers knew the gallery images were AI-made.
